summary.text: At \(n=140\), consecutive-square bounds determine \(a(140)=471\), \(a(144)=484\), \(a(157)=528\), and \(a(161)=542\). Thus the proposed right-hand side is \(528+484-471=541\), not \(542\), giving a counterexample.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=2n+\left\lfloor n\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac n4\right\rfloor,
\qquad n\ge 1.
\]
We disprove the proposed recurrence
\[
a(n+21)=a(n+17)+a(n+4)-a(n)
\]
by exhibiting a counterexample at \(n=140\).

We will need the values of \(a(140),a(144),a(157)\), and \(a(161)\). To evaluate their irrational floor terms exactly, use the following elementary observation. If \(m\) and \(z\) are nonnegative integers and
\[
z^2\le m^2\frac54<(z+1)^2,
\]
then
\[
z\le m\sqrt{\frac54}<z+1,
\]
and hence
\[
\left\lfloor m\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=z.
\]
Indeed, all quantities being compared are nonnegative, so squaring preserves their order, and
\[
\left(m\sqrt{\frac54}\right)^2=m^2\frac54.
\]
Thus the two displayed squared inequalities are exactly the squared forms of the inequalities needed to identify the floor.

We now perform the four required evaluations.

First, for \(m=140\),
\[
140^2\frac54=19600\cdot\frac54=24500.
\]
Moreover,
\[
156^2=24336\le 24500<24649=157^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\left\lfloor 140\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=156.
\]
Also \(\lfloor 140/4\rfloor=35\). Consequently,
\[
a(140)=2\cdot140+156+35=280+156+35=471.
\]

Second, for \(m=144\),
\[
144^2\frac54=20736\cdot\frac54=25920.
\]
Here
\[
160^2=25600\le25920<25921=161^2.
\]
It follows that
\[
\left\lfloor 144\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=160.
\]
Since \(\lfloor144/4\rfloor=36\), we get
\[
a(144)=2\cdot144+160+36=288+160+36=484.
\]

Third, for \(m=157\),
\[
157^2\frac54=24649\cdot\frac54=\frac{123245}{4}=30811\frac14.
\]
The neighboring relevant squares satisfy
\[
175^2=30625\le \frac{123245}{4}<30976=176^2.
\]
For completeness, these inequalities can be checked without decimals by multiplying through by \(4\):
\[
122500\le123245<123904.
\]
Hence
\[
\left\lfloor157\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=175.
\]
Furthermore, \(157=4\cdot39+1\), so \(\lfloor157/4\rfloor=39\). Therefore
\[
a(157)=2\cdot157+175+39=314+175+39=528.
\]

Finally, for \(m=161\),
\[
161^2\frac54=25921\cdot\frac54=\frac{129605}{4}=32401\frac14.
\]
We have
\[
180^2=32400\le\frac{129605}{4}<32761=181^2.
\]
Equivalently, after multiplication by \(4\),
\[
129600\le129605<131044.
\]
Thus
\[
\left\lfloor161\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=180.
\]
As \(161=4\cdot40+1\), we also have \(\lfloor161/4\rfloor=40\). It follows that
\[
a(161)=2\cdot161+180+40=322+180+40=542.
\]

Now apply the conjectured identity at the admissible index \(n=140\). Since
\[
140+21=161,\qquad 140+17=157,\qquad 140+4=144,
\]
it would assert
\[
a(161)=a(157)+a(144)-a(140).
\]
But the values just established give
\[
a(157)+a(144)-a(140)=528+484-471=1012-471=541,
\]
whereas
\[
a(161)=542.
\]
Thus the proposed equality would require \(542=541\), which is false. Therefore the recurrence fails at \(n=140\), and the conjecture that it holds for every \(n\ge1\) is disproved.
